prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with B026 first and B049 third, and after reading all eight ballots I now put B049 first. It is an instrument-and-measurement achievement with a clean origin (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice proposal and first strontium clock), a demonstrated record (Ye's JILA programme taking stability and accuracy to the 10^-18 regime), and independent confirmation by many national laboratories and by direct clock-to-clock comparisons. Four colleagues (Kroll, Lindroth, Danielsson, Johansson) independently describe the credit as a natural pair, and Lindroth and Kroll judge the atomic-structure physics (polarizabilities, blackbody shifts, clock transitions) from inside the field. The science has consequences beyond metrology: tests of constant variation and relativistic time dilation over millimetre scales, relativistic geodesy, and a concrete path to redefining the second. It is mature and timely, and the attribution does not need to be forced.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty against earlier precision-measurement prizes: 2005 (combs, Hall and Haensch) and 2012 (Wineland, controlled single quantum systems, including the Al+ ion clock) cover the enabling technology, and Ye was trained in the comb tradition. The clocks so far deliver null tests of fundamental physics rather than a new physical discovery, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. A committee could reasonably judge that the field is partly recognised already, or that a better-defined discovery such as B009 or B026 gives more new physics per prize. Pierre Lemonde, Ludlow and others also have credible claims to parts of the lattice-clock story, so a two-name prize is clean on paper but not uncontested.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B009 first as a clean theory-plus-experiment discovery (Bistritzer-MacDonald flat bands, Jarillo-Herrero's correlated and superconducting states) that opened moire quantum matter, and he also placed B049 second and B026 third while flagging the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of B026: the missing HgTe proposers are a real allocation problem and it moved me off my own opening first choice. On B009 I disagree about timing rather than merit. The pairing mechanism is unsettled and the field is eight years old, and both Eriksson and Mehlig concede the interpretation is still moving. I rate B009 as a very strong candidate that gains from waiting, while B049 has no comparable open interpretive question. I would still keep B009 as an alternative, since his observation that it is easy to state and well delineated is correct.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B049 first, saying the clocks rest on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's high-stability strontium work, that the atomic-structure physics is something she can judge directly, and that over twenty years of independent confirmation make recognition timely.
responses.response: I find this persuasive, and her assessment of the polarizability and blackbody-shift physics is exactly the expertise I lack, so I give it weight. Her own uncertainty about weighing the work against 2005 and 2012 is the main thing I want to test in discussion. My view is that the 2012 prize was for manipulating individual quantum systems and the 2005 prize for the comb as a frequency ruler. The lattice clock is a separate idea that makes the interrogation of many atoms at the same time compatible with an unperturbed transition, which is what moved accuracy by orders of magnitude. I would want her to say whether she sees any weakness in that distinction.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B009 first and B026 second, with strong praise for the clean theory-to-experiment chain in twisted graphene and the Z2 classification, while noting that credit for B026 omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological insulator contributors.
responses.response: His B026 qualification is the one I take most seriously because he does not dismiss it: Zhang's death and the 2D versus 3D split mean that a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves out people whose contributions were decisive for the experiment being done at all. I therefore no longer put B026 first, although I still think it is conceptually the deeper result. I disagree that its recognition is clearly overdue enough to accept an imperfect trio; if the committee can find a fair framing around the quantum spin Hall effect specifically, it would return as my first choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked active-matter hydrodynamics (B011) first, valuing the unified conceptual framework from Vicsek, Toner-Tu and Ramaswamy, but acknowledged that Yuhai Tu is missing and that the prize might be seen as living-matter rather than mainstream statistical physics.
responses.response: I respect the originality of the theory, but I do not think B011 is ready as a physics prize. He himself says the exact Toner-Tu exponents are confirmed in only a few systems, and no other member ranks it. The omission of Tu from a Toner-Tu result is also a defect in the attribution that I do not see how to repair within three names. I would want to hear what decisive experiment he regards as having tested the central prediction before moving B011 up.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B040 (circuit QED) first, as an original and clean architecture behind superconducting processors, but flagged overlap with, and proximity to, the 2025 circuit prize and his own closeness to the field.
responses.response: I appreciate that he stated his bias openly. I share his timing worry: two prizes on superconducting circuits within about two years would leave the committee open to the charge of concentrating on one community, and I note that Kroll and Lindroth both make the same point. This is not a disagreement about the science, and circuit QED may well deserve a prize later. It is a reason not to lead with it now, and a reason that makes B049 a better choice for this year.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B049 first and B012 second, describing the lattice clock as laser cooling, trapping and spectroscopy producing the most accurate measurements humans make, and doubting the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes only mildly.
responses.response: I agree on the central point. I would only qualify his view by flagging that his record-accuracy claim, which he says he has not verified, is the weakest part of the credit argument for Ye, and I would ask that the committee check the specific stability and uncertainty numbers rather than rely on general knowledge. He also ranks B012 second with an unresolved Cirac versus Greiner choice, which is why I keep it out of my alternatives: the credit problem is genuinely harder than for B049.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Ludlow or another early lattice-clock contributor has a decisive claim that would require a third name.
How strongly the 2005 and 2012 prizes should weigh against this work as part of the same precision-measurement lineage.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before awarding.
Whether a fair framing of B026 can be found that deals with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D topological insulator questions, since that would change my ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B049 or for the alternatives B026 and B009, which are outside my fields (atomic clocks and condensed matter). My profile does record astroparticle and gamma-ray instrumentation work (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+, XL-Calibur), so if B047 (IceCube neutrinos) were to be seriously considered I would flag a professional proximity and consider recusing myself from that item.
